title: OPRE 3333: Time Series & Forecasting Exam Reference

examFormat.mix: Multiple choice, short answer calculations, and multi-part problems involving forecasting and regression.
examFormat.notes: No notes or books allowed. Calculator is required.

verifiedPatterns.pattern: ★ Calculate MAE, MSE, and MAPE for a given time series using Naive, Average, Moving Average, or Exponential Smoothing methods.
★ Use a given multiple regression equation (with trend and/or seasonal dummies) to compute forecasts for future periods (e.g., 'next year').
★ Set up and interpret a multiple regression model with dummy variables to account for seasonality and trend.
★ Choose the best forecasting model by comparing accuracy metrics (e.g., MSE) between different methods or parameters (e.g., Moving Average k=3 vs k=5).

topics.name: Time Series Forecasting Methods
topics.why: Core of the exam. You must be able to calculate forecasts using Naive, Average, Moving Average, and Exponential Smoothing.
topics.src: exam-review-2.pdf Q12, Q13, Q14, Q15; lecture-06.pdf p7-13

topics.name: Forecast Accuracy Metrics
topics.why: Every calculation problem asks for MAE, MSE, or MAPE. Know the formulas and what they measure.
topics.src: exam-review-2.pdf Q12, Q13, Q14, Q15; lecture-06.pdf p6

topics.name: Regression for Forecasting
topics.why: The most complex problems involve building or using regression models with trend and seasonal dummy variables.
topics.src: exam-review-2.pdf Q16, Q17, Q18, Q19; lecture-06.pdf p16-23

topics.name: Time Series Patterns
topics.why: Identifying the pattern (Horizontal, Trend, Seasonal) is the first step to choosing the correct forecasting method.
topics.src: exam-review-2.pdf Q9, Q10, Q11; lecture-06.pdf p2-5

topics.name: Interpreting Regression Output
topics.why: You need to read ANOVA and Coefficients tables to assess model significance (F-test, p-values) and understand predictor effects (coefficients, t-stats).

topics.name: Data Visualization
topics.why: Conceptual questions test when to use specific charts (Bar, Column, Line, Scatter, Crosstab).
topics.src: exam-review-2.pdf Q3, Q4, Q5; lecture-05.pdf p1-4

formulas.name: ★ Naive Forecast
formulas.vars: ŷ_{t+1} forecast for next period · y_t actual value for current period
formulas.when: For a horizontal pattern, as a simple baseline.

formulas.name: ★ Average of All Data Forecast
formulas.vars: ŷ_{t+1} forecast for next period · y_i historical values · t number of periods
formulas.when: For a stable horizontal pattern with no trend.

formulas.name: ★ Moving Average Forecast
formulas.vars: k number of periods in average · y_t most recent value
formulas.when: For a horizontal pattern where only recent values are relevant.

formulas.name: ★ Exponential Smoothing Forecast
formulas.vars: α smoothing constant (0-1) · y_t current actual · ŷ_t current forecast
formulas.when: For a horizontal pattern. A weighted average approach.
formulas.trap: The first forecast ŷ₂ is set to the first actual value y₁.

formulas.name: Forecast Error
formulas.vars: e_t error · y_t actual value · ŷ_t forecasted value
formulas.when: Always the first step for calculating accuracy metrics.
formulas.ex: Actual y₅=298, Forecast ŷ₅=310. Error e₅ = 298 - 310 = -12. ✓

formulas.name: ★ Mean Absolute Error (MAE)
formulas.vars: e_t forecast error · n number of forecasts
formulas.when: To find the average forecast error magnitude in original units.

formulas.name: ★ Mean Squared Error (MSE)
formulas.vars: e_t forecast error · n number of forecasts
formulas.when: To measure accuracy, heavily penalizing large errors.

formulas.name: ★ Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE)
formulas.vars: e_t error · y_t actual value · n number of forecasts
formulas.when: To find average percentage error, useful for comparing across different scales.
formulas.ex: y₂=287, e₂=53. |e₂/y₂| = |53/287| = 0.1847. Sum these percentages and divide by n.

formulas.name: ★ Linear Trend Regression Forecast
formulas.vars: ŷ_t forecast · b₀ intercept · b₁ slope · t time period
formulas.when: Forecasting data with a consistent linear trend.

formulas.name: ★ Seasonal Regression (No Trend)
formulas.vars: b₀ base case (Qtr4) avg · b₁,b₂,b₃ adjustments for other qtrs
formulas.when: Data has a repeating seasonal pattern but no long-term trend.
formulas.ex: Eq: ŷ=77-10Q1-30Q2-20Q3. Forecast Q2: 77-30=47. Forecast Q4: 77. ✓

formulas.name: ★ Seasonal Regression (With Trend)
formulas.formula: ŷ_t = b₀ + b₁Qtr1 + b₂Qtr2 + b₃Qtr3 + b₄t
formulas.vars: b₀ intercept at t=0 for base qtr · b₁,b₂,b₃ seasonal adjustments · b₄ trend slope · t time period
formulas.when: Data has both seasonal patterns and a linear trend.

formulas.name: R Square (R²)
formulas.vars: SS_Regression explained variation · SS_Total total variation
formulas.when: To measure the percentage of variation in Y explained by the model's X variables.
formulas.ex: R²=0.928 means 92.8% of the variation in the dependent variable is explained by the model. ✓

formulas.name: ★ MFE (Mean Forecast Error)
formulas.vars: eₜ: forecast error (Actual - Forecast) for period t · n: number of periods with forecasts
formulas.when: To measure the average bias of a forecast. A large positive or negative value indicates consistent over- or under-forecasting.
formulas.trap: Relying on MFE alone is WRONG because positive and negative errors can cancel out, making a biased forecast look good. MFE=0 does not mean the forecast is accurate, just that it's unbiased.
formulas.ex: Errors: -10, 5, -10, 5, 10. Sum = 0. MFE = 0/5 = 0. The forecast is unbiased. ✓ (NOT an indicator of low error, as MAE is 8).

formulas.name: ★ Forecast for Next Period (Moving Avg)
formulas.vars: ŷₜ₊₁: forecast for the next period · yₜ: actual value in period t · k: number of periods in the moving average
formulas.when: Forecasting for a time series with a horizontal pattern (no trend or seasonality).

formulas.name: ★ Forecast for Next Period (Exp. Smoothing)
formulas.vars: ŷₜ₊₁: forecast for next period · α: smoothing constant · yₜ: actual value at t · ŷₜ: forecast at t
formulas.when: Forecasting for a time series with a horizontal pattern, giving more weight to recent data.

formulas.name: ★ Forecast for Next Period (Linear Trend)
formulas.vars: ŷₜ: forecast for period t · b₀: intercept · b₁: slope · t: time period index
formulas.when: Forecasting for a time series with a clear linear trend.

formulas.name: ★ Forecast for Next Quarter (Seasonal + Trend)
formulas.formula: ŷₜ = b₀ + b₁Qtr1 + b₂Qtr2 + b₃Qtr3 + b₄t
formulas.vars: b₀: intercept · b₁,b₂,b₃: seasonal effects · b₄: trend effect · t: time period index
formulas.when: Forecasting for a time series with both seasonality and a linear trend.

formulas.name: ★ Forecast for Next Quarter (Seasonal Only)
formulas.vars: b₀: intercept (base quarter value) · b₁,b₂,b₃: adjustments for other quarters
formulas.when: Forecasting for a time series with seasonality but no trend.
formulas.ex: Model: ŷ = 77 - 10Q1 - 30Q2 - 20Q3. Forecast for Q2: ŷ = 77 - 30(1) = 47 ✓. Forecast for Q4 (base): ŷ = 77 ✓.

formulas.name: ★ Full Seasonal + Trend Model Equation
formulas.formula: ŷₜ = b₀ + b₁Qtr1 + b₂Qtr2 + b₃Qtr3 + b₄·Period
formulas.vars: b₀ intercept · b₁-b₃ seasonal coeffs · b₄ trend coeff · Period is time index t
formulas.when: Building a predictive model from scratch for data with both seasonal and trend patterns.

formulas.name: Residual Sum of Squares (SSE or Residual SS)
formulas.vars: yᵢ: actual value · ŷᵢ: predicted value from regression
formulas.when: Calculating the unexplained variance in a regression model. This is the value the model seeks to minimize.
formulas.ex: From ANOVA table: Residual SS = 35.62. This is the sum of all squared forecast errors for the 10 observations. ✓

formulas.name: ★ Forecast for Specific Quarter (Seasonal+Trend)
formulas.formula: ŷ_t = b₀ + b₁(Qtr1) + b₂(Qtr2) + b₃(Qtr3) + b₄(t)
formulas.vars: b₀..b₄ are coefficients · Qtr1..3 are dummy variables · t is the time period
formulas.when: Forecasting a time series with both a seasonal pattern and a linear trend.
formulas.trap: Forgetting to set the correct dummy variables to 0 for the quarter you are forecasting is a common error.

formulas.name: ★ Forecast for Next Period (Average of All)
formulas.vars: y_t is the actual value at period t · t is the number of past periods
formulas.when: Time series has a horizontal pattern with no trend or seasonality.

formulas.name: t-Statistic for Coefficient
formulas.vars: Coefficient is the estimated slope or intercept · Standard Error is its uncertainty
formulas.when: Testing if a single predictor variable is statistically significant (i.e., its coefficient is different from zero).
formulas.trap: A t-stat less than ~2 (in absolute value) is generally NOT statistically significant at the 95% confidence level.
formulas.ex: From regression output: Coefficient=2.3618, Std Error=0.2323. t Stat = 2.3618 / 0.2323 = 10.17 ✓. Since |10.17| > 2, the variable is highly significant.

formulas.name: F-Statistic (ANOVA)
formulas.vars: MS_Regression is Mean Square of Regression · MS_Residual is Mean Square of Residuals (or Errors)
formulas.when: Testing the overall significance of the entire regression model.
formulas.trap: A high F-statistic is good, but you must check its p-value (Significance F). A low p-value (< 0.05) confirms the model is significant.
formulas.ex: From ANOVA table: MS_Regression = 460.20, MS_Residual = 4.45. F = 460.20 / 4.45 = 103.35 ✓. The associated p-value was 7.5E-06, so the model is significant.

formulas.name: Adjusted R-Square
formulas.vars: R² is R-Square · n is number of observations · p is number of predictors
formulas.when: Comparing regression models with different numbers of predictor variables.
formulas.trap: Adjusted R² can be negative if the model is worse than predicting the mean, which is a strong signal the model is very poor.

formulas.name: Standard Error of Regression
formulas.vars: SSE is Sum of Squared Residuals · n is observations · p is predictors · MS_Residual is Mean Square Residual
formulas.when: To measure the typical distance between observed values and the regression line, in the units of the Y variable.
formulas.ex: From ANOVA table, MS_Residual = 4.4527. Standard Error = √4.4527 = 2.11 ✓. Predictions are typically off by ±2.11 units.

formulas.name: Alternative Exponential Smoothing Formula
formulas.vars: ŷ_t is the forecast for period t · α is the smoothing constant · e_t is the forecast error for period t (y_t - ŷ_t)
formulas.when: Updating a forecast based on the most recent error. Conceptually shows how the model 'learns'.
formulas.ex: Given ŷ₂=17, y₂=21, α=0.2. First find error e₂ = 21-17=4. Then forecast for period 3 is ŷ₃ = 17 + 0.2 * 4 = 17.8 ✓

formulas.name: Mean Square (MS) in ANOVA
formulas.vars: SS is the Sum of Squares for a source (Regression or Residual) · df is the degrees of freedom for that source
formulas.when: Calculating the F-statistic. It represents the average variation.
formulas.ex: From ANOVA table: SS_Regression = 460.2, df_Regression = 1. MS_Regression = 460.2 / 1 = 460.2 ✓

concepts.def: A set of observations on a variable measured at successive, regular points in time (e.g., daily sales, quarterly profits).
Data fluctuates randomly around a constant mean over time. No trend or seasonality.
A gradual, long-term shift to higher or lower values. Can be linear or non-linear.
A recurring pattern of highs and lows that completes within a year and repeats annually (e.g., winter coat sales).
Variables coded as 0 or 1 to represent categorical data (like seasons) in a regression model. For k categories, you must use k-1 dummy variables.
In exponential smoothing, the weight (0 to 1) given to the most recent actual value. High α reacts quickly to changes; low α provides more smoothing.
The number of recent periods used to calculate the forecast. A small k tracks shifts quickly but is sensitive to noise; a large k is smoother.
Techniques that use models constructed from past data to predict the future or ascertain the impact of one variable on another.
Techniques that describe what has happened in the past, such as data visualization and summary statistics.
Techniques that yield a best course of action to take. Optimization models are a key example.
A tabular summary of data for two variables, often used to show the relationship between one categorical and one quantitative variable, or two categorical variables.
The coefficient of determination. Measures the proportion of variance in the dependent variable that is predictable from the independent variable(s).
A modified version of R² that adjusts for the number of predictors in a model. It penalizes for adding non-significant variables.
In ANOVA, tests the overall significance of the regression model. It compares the model's explanatory power to a model with no independent variables.
The probability of observing the F-statistic if the null hypothesis (that all model coefficients are zero) is true. A p-value < 0.05 indicates a statistically significant model.
Tests the significance of an individual regression coefficient. It's the coefficient divided by its standard error. A |t Stat| > 2 is a rule of thumb for significance at the 95% level.
The typical distance between the observed values and the regression line. It is a measure of the model's predictive accuracy in the units of the dependent variable.
Charts that use horizontal (bar) or vertical (column) bars to display and compare the frequency or magnitude of categorical variables.
The average of all forecast errors (Actual - Forecast). Its primary use is to identify systematic bias. A value far from zero implies a consistent tendency to over- or under-forecast.

concepts.def: A graph showing the relationship between two quantitative variables. One variable is plotted on the horizontal axis and the other on the vertical axis. Used to spot correlations and trends.
A chart that connects a series of data points with a continuous line. It is the primary tool for visualizing time series data to identify patterns like trend and seasonality.
The correlation coefficient between the actual values (Y) and the predicted values (Ŷ) from a regression model. It ranges from -1 to +1 and measures the strength of the linear relationship.
A measure of total variance in a dataset. Total SS = Regression SS (explained variance) + Residual SS (unexplained variance). Found in the ANOVA table.
The average variance, calculated as Sum of Squares (SS) divided by its degrees of freedom (df). The F-statistic is the ratio of MS Regression to MS Residual.
The number of values in a final calculation that are free to vary. For regression residuals, df = n - p - 1, where n is observations and p is the number of predictors.
A minimalist line chart placed in a single cell, showing a general trend without axes. Useful for compact data visualization in tables.
A variation of a scatter chart that visualizes three variables in two dimensions. The x and y axes represent two variables, while the size of the bubble represents the third.
A graphical representation of data where values are depicted by color. Often used on tables to quickly identify high and low values.
A time series pattern showing rises and falls that are not of a fixed period, often lasting multiple years. These fluctuations are usually due to multi-year economic or business cycles.
A form of prescriptive analytics that aims to identify the best possible decision from a set of alternatives, given certain constraints. It helps find the maximum profit, minimum cost, etc.
A range (e.g., Lower 95%, Upper 95%) that likely contains the true value of a regression coefficient. If the interval does not contain 0, the coefficient is statistically significant.
A line on a scatter chart that provides an approximation of the relationship between two quantitative variables. It helps visualize the direction and strength of a trend.
A predictive analytics technique used to find patterns, relationships, and anomalies in large databases. It's about discovering insights, not just describing data.
A predictive analytics technique that uses probability and statistics to build a computer model to study the impact of uncertainty on a decision.
Numerical or quantitative data where all arithmetic operations (add, subtract, multiply, divide) are meaningful. Examples include height, price, and temperature.
Qualitative or categorical data where values are labels or names. Arithmetic operations are meaningless. Examples include marital status or product category.
The portion of the total variation in the dependent variable (Y) that is explained by the regression model. Appears as 'SS' in the 'Regression' row of the ANOVA table.

traps.text: Using k dummy variables for k categories is WRONG because it introduces perfect multicollinearity, making the regression model unsolvable. Always use k-1 dummy variables.
Applying smoothing methods (Moving Avg, Exp. Smoothing) to data with a clear trend is WRONG because these methods are for horizontal patterns and will consistently lag behind the trend.
Choosing a model based only on R² is INCORRECT because R² always increases when you add variables, even useless ones. Use Adjusted R² to compare models with different numbers of predictors.
Relying on MFE alone is WRONG because positive and negative errors can cancel out, making a biased forecast look accurate. An MFE of 0 does NOT mean the forecast is perfect.
A negative Adjusted R² is NOT an error. It indicates the model is worse than a simple horizontal line (predicting the mean), meaning the chosen predictors have no explanatory power.
Confusing MAE and MSE is a common mistake. MSE penalizes large errors more heavily than MAE because it squares the errors. The choice is NOT arbitrary; it depends on how costly large errors are.

Interpreting the intercept coefficient when the predictor variable (e.g., time) cannot be zero is WRONG. For a time series starting at Year 1, the intercept (at Year 0) is a mathematical anchor, not a practical prediction.
Assuming a small `k` in moving averages is always better is FALSE. A small `k` tracks shifts faster but is very sensitive to random noise; a larger `k` provides more smoothing for volatile data.
Assuming a large `α` in exponential smoothing is always better is FALSE. A large `α` reacts quickly to real changes but will overreact to random noise. Use a small `α` for noisy data.

Assuming a high R² means the model is good for forecasting is FALSE. A high R² indicates a good fit for past data, but it doesn't guarantee future predictive accuracy, especially if the model is overfit.
Using a line chart for categorical comparisons is WRONG. Line charts imply a connection or trend over time between points. Use bar or column charts for comparing distinct categories.
Using Adjusted R² to compare models on different datasets is INCORRECT. Adjusted R² is only valid for comparing models fit to the exact same set of observations (Y values).
★ Interpreting a seasonal dummy coefficient as the season's absolute forecast is WRONG. The coefficient is the average difference *relative to the base quarter* (the one with no dummy variable).

★ Using a seasonal-only regression model when a clear trend exists is INCORRECT. This will produce poor forecasts because the model's average (the intercept) does not change over time, failing to capture the underlying growth or decline.

★ Forgetting to increment the time variable `t` for future forecasts in a trend model is a common WRONG step. If your data ends at t=12, the next year's forecasts use t=13, 14, 15, 16, not t=1, 2, 3, 4.

Assuming a non-significant p-value for one dummy variable (e.g., Qtr1) means seasonality is NOT present is FALSE. It only means that quarter is not statistically different from the base quarter (e.g., Qtr4). Other quarters might be very different.

Interpreting a regression intercept like 'Sales at Year 0' is often WRONG if Year 0 is far outside the range of your data. The intercept is primarily a mathematical anchor for the line, not always a meaningful real-world value.
★ Using a bar chart to show a relationship between two quantitative variables is WRONG because bar charts are for comparing categorical variables; a scatter chart is the correct tool.
★ Including non-significant seasonal dummy variables (with high p-values > 0.05) in a final model is WRONG because they add complexity without explanatory power and can worsen forecast accuracy.
Choosing the moving average order 'k' without testing is WRONG because the optimal 'k' that minimizes MSE depends on the specific time series data; it must be found by comparison.
Choosing the exponential smoothing constant 'α' without testing is WRONG because the optimal 'α' that minimizes MSE depends on the balance of trend and noise in the data.

Ignoring the F-statistic's p-value (Significance F) is WRONG because even if individual coefficients seem significant, a high p-value for the F-test (> 0.05) means the overall model is not statistically reliable.
